findings.issue_text: `queued` dataclass default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so all instances share a stale timestamp; should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`
`queued` datetime is serialized as a string through the Celery round-trip and `from_dict` doesn't parse/validate it, breaking the dataclass contract
`from_dict` returns None on malformed input, silently reverting to user-initiated assignment and re-enabling sync cycles instead of failing loudly
`should_sync(self, attribute)` signature change breaks existing subclass overrides that still use the old single-parameter signature, causing TypeError in the sync task

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` dataclass default is evaluated once at import time in AssignmentSource (src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:16), so every instance created via `from_integration` gets the process's import timestamp, making the 'queued' timestamp meaningless for staleness/dedup logic

`to_dict()` emits a raw `datetime` object in Celery task kwargs (`sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(..., assignment_source_dict=assignment_source.to_dict())` in sync.py), which is not JSON-serializable with the default JSON task serializer, causing every outbound assignee sync carrying an assignment source to fail at task dispatch
`assignment_source.to_dict()` is computed inside the loop over `external_issue_ids` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:137–142) and should be hoisted out of the loop as a trivial cleanup

In assignment_source.py:17, the `queued` dataclass field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition time rather than per instance, so every `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` gets process startup time instead of creation time; should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` or set it in `from_integration`.

In assignment_source.py:26 and sync.py:140, `to_dict()` keeps `queued` as a datetime object and the dict is passed via `apply_async(kwargs=...)`, which will raise a serialization error under a JSON broker/serializer so the `sync_assignee_outbound` task never enqueues and assignment sync silently dies; the `queued` timestamp should be dropped from the payload or serialized explicitly.

In assignment_source.py:33-36, `from_dict` returns `None` on malformed payloads and `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` proceeds with the sync, silently re-enabling the sync loop the PR is meant to prevent; a parse failure should fail safe (skip the sync) or at least log/alert. Additionally, `from_dict` accepts arbitrary types (e.g. `integration_id="abc"`) without validation, only catching structural errors.

In issues.py:66, the base `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` gained a new `sync_source` parameter, but any subclass still overriding with the old signature `def should_sync(self, attribute)` will raise a TypeError when called with `sync_source=` as a keyword, crashing assignment sync for that provider at runtime.

In issues.py:382-392, cycle prevention covers assignee sync only — status sync remains unprotected: `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source` parameter but no caller passes it and no guard uses it, so in a multi-integration mirror an inbound status change can reproduce the sync loop this PR claims to fix.

In sync_assignee_outbound.py, the task body has no guard against `Integration.DoesNotExist` raised mid-flight by `integration_service.get_integration(...)`, causing indefinite retries; combined with the new `from_dict` returning None, a malformed payload yields no observability at all.

No end-to-end cycle test for the core feature: no test exercises sync_group_assignee_inbound followed by sync_group_assignee_outbound to verify the sync cycle is actually broken across the full pipeline (task → sync util → model → mixin), so a regression in any hop (e.g., forgetting to pass assignment_source through sync_group_assignee_outbound kwargs) would not be caught

No test that a different integration's assignment source still propagates outward: the should_sync guard only blocks matching integration_id, and the claimed behavior 'still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' is untested — a too-aggressive guard (e.g., 'if sync_source: return False') would pass the existing test suite; need a test with two linked integrations where an assignment from integration A still syncs to integration B

No direct unit test for should_sync behavior, including the None and falsy-source edge cases (sync_source=None falling through to config check, sync_source.integration_id == None mismatch, non-matching id), and no test verifying behavior when org_integration is set but integration ids differ in type (RpcIntegration vs int)

Missing test that assignment_source_dict survives Celery serialization: AssignmentSource.queued defaults to timezone.now() at class-definition (import) time not per instance, tests only assert queued is not None and never check JSON-serializability or accurate timestamps, and eager-mode self.tasks() bypasses real queue serialization — a round-trip test (e.g., json.dumps(assignment_source.to_dict())) is missing

Behavioral change to abstract sync_status_outbound signature to accept assignment_source with no test work: there are no tests for status sync with an assignment source and no caller in the diff actually passes it for status sync — dead API surface or incomplete wiring shipped untested

from_dict round-trip test doesn't cover the full serialized payload: test_from_dict_valid_data builds the dict by hand rather than using to_dict() output, so from_dict(source.to_dict()) including the queued datetime is never tested — if queued serialization breaks, from_dict(to_dict(...)) could yield queued as a str instead of datetime, flowing undetected into should_sync callers

adjudication_records.issue_text: `queued` datetime is serialized as a string through the Celery round-trip and `from_dict` doesn't parse/validate it, breaking the dataclass contract

adjudication.rationale: `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` uses `asdict(self)` so it includes `queued` (a `datetime`) in the payload. That dict is passed through Celery in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` as `assignment_source_dict` (via `apply_async(kwargs={...})`). On the receiving side, `AssignmentSource.from_dict` simply does `cls(**input_dict)` and only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError`, so if Celery serializes `queued` to a string (or otherwise changes its type), it will be accepted without parsing/validation and `queued` will no longer be a `datetime`. This breaks the intended dataclass contract and can cause downstream type/logic issues (and may also break task serialization depending on Celery serializer).

adjudication_records.issue_text: `from_dict` returns None on malformed input, silently reverting to user-initiated assignment and re-enabling sync cycles instead of failing loudly

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AssignmentSource.from_dict` intentionally returns `None` on malformed input (catching `ValueError`/`TypeError`), and `sync_assignee_outbound` then passes that `None` into `installation.should_sync(...)`. Since the new cycle-prevention in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` only triggers when `sync_source` is non-`None` and matches the integration id, a malformed `assignment_source_dict` would bypass the cycle check and allow outbound sync. However, the diff also shows the only new internal producer uses `assignment_source.to_dict()` (well-formed), and returning `None` is explicitly tested, so this is more a robustness/design concern than a proven defect in the shown changes.

This is an API/signature change that would indeed raise `TypeError` at runtime for any existing integration installation subclass that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-parameter signature. However, the diff does not show any such subclass override, so the breakage is a compatibility risk rather than a verifiable defect within the shown changes.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`, the dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. As a result, every `AssignmentSource(...)` created without an explicit `queued` value (including `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)`) will share the same timestamp (process startup/import time) rather than the actual creation time. The correct pattern is `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` or setting `queued` inside the constructor/from_integration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `queued` default uses `timezone.now()` evaluated once at module import time instead of `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`, so every AssignmentSource gets the import timestamp

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`, the dataclass defines `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. That calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/module import time, so all `AssignmentSource` instances created without an explicit `queued` will share the same timestamp (the import time). For per-instance timestamps it should use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `to_dict()` leaves `queued` as a datetime object, which fails JSON serialization when passed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(...)` with the default JSON serializer

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` returning `asdict(self)`, which will include `queued` as a `datetime` object, and that dict is passed into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(...)`. However, the claim that this "fails JSON serialization with the default JSON serializer" is not verifiable from the diff: the serializer configuration is not shown, and Celery/Kombu JSON serialization commonly supports datetimes via a custom encoder. So the asserted failure mode is not established by the changes shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `from_dict` doesn't validate types, so `queued` and `integration_id` can silently become strings and propagate bad values

adjudication.rationale: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` just does `cls(**input_dict)` and only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError`; Python dataclasses don’t enforce the annotated types at runtime. So inputs like `{ "integration_id": "123" }` or `{ "queued": "..." }` will successfully construct an `AssignmentSource` with wrong types. That can directly break the new sync-cycle prevention in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` (`sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`) because a string vs int comparison will fail, allowing cycles to occur.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `sync_status_outbound` abstractmethod signature adds an `assignment_source` parameter that is never used by any caller — dead API surface or incomplete change leaving status sync with the same cycle risk

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `assignment_source` is threaded through the assignee outbound path (task parses `assignment_source_dict`, `should_sync(..., parsed_assignment_source)`, and `sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)`). By contrast, `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter but no corresponding call sites are updated here to pass it, nor is `should_sync` shown being called for status with a source. This makes the new status parameter effectively unused in the shown changes and suggests the cycle-prevention work was only completed for assignee sync, leaving status sync potentially unaddressed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Layering leak: `GroupAssignee` model imports `sentry.integrations.services.assignment_source` at module scope, widening the integration dependency into the ORM manager's signature

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py` adding a module-scope import `from sentry.integrations.services.assignment_source import AssignmentSource` and threading `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` through the ORM manager methods `assign(...)` and `deassign(...)`. This concretely widens the models/ORM layer API to depend on an integrations service type, matching the stated “layering leak” concern. It’s an architectural coupling issue introduced by this change, not a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `assignment_source` is manually converted between AssignmentSource and dict across five signatures/layers instead of using a single serialization helper or passing the object to the task

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` / `from_dict()` as the single serialization helper (see new `assignment_source.py`), and uses it only at the task boundary: `sync_group_assignee_outbound(...)->apply_async(kwargs={"assignment_source_dict": assignment_source.to_dict()...})` and `sync_assignee_outbound(...)->AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)`. Other layers pass the typed `AssignmentSource | None` through (`GroupAssignee.assign/deassign`, `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, `sync_assignee_outbound` call). So it’s not “manually converted across five signatures/layers” nor lacking a single helper; it’s already centralized and limited to Celery-serializable dict at the boundary.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `source_name` is stored but never used for logic (cycle detection uses only `integration_id`), adding dead serialization surface that can go stale

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, cycle detection logic in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` only checks `sync_source.integration_id` against `self.org_integration.integration_id` and does not use `source_name` at all. `AssignmentSource` still serializes/deserializes `source_name` via `to_dict()`/`from_dict()` and passes it through task kwargs (`assignment_source_dict`), so the finding that `source_name` is stored but unused for logic is accurate. This is not a correctness defect, but it is extra serialized surface/maintenance overhead that could drift over time.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test contains stale copy-pasted assertions spliced mid-function, and the `assignment_source=None` mock assertion would pass even if task argument plumbing regressed

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not show any “stale copy-pasted assertions spliced mid-function” defect in the tests; the added assertions in `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign` are coherent and placed after the mock call check. Also, the claim that asserting `assignment_source=None` “would pass even if task argument plumbing regressed” is not supported: the task `sync_assignee_outbound` now explicitly calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, and `assert_called_with(..., assignment_source=None)` would fail if that kwarg were omitted or renamed. The new second test additionally exercises the non-None source path to prevent sync cycles.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AssignmentSource.queued default datetime is evaluated once at import time, so all instances share the same timestamp, making the diagnostic field misleading

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` (new file `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`), the dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. This calls `timezone.now()` at import/class definition time, so every `AssignmentSource()` created without an explicit `queued` will share the same timestamp value. For per-instance timestamps, it should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: to_dict() keeps queued as a datetime object which is not JSON-serializable, causing sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async to crash under the JSON Celery serializer, breaking cross-integration propagation

adjudication.rationale: `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which includes the `queued: datetime` field as a raw `datetime` object (see `assignment_source.py`). That dict is passed directly into Celery task kwargs in `sync_group_assignee_outbound()` via `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(..., assignment_source_dict=assignment_source.to_dict())` (see `integrations/utils/sync.py`). If the Celery serializer is JSON (common), a `datetime` in kwargs is not JSON-serializable and would cause task enqueue/serialization to fail, breaking outbound propagation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: from_dict silently returns None on deserialization failure, bypassing the should_sync cycle-prevention check and allowing sync loops

adjudication.rationale: In `sync_assignee_outbound`, `parsed_assignment_source = AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)` and then `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` is used. In `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, the cycle-prevention guard only triggers when `sync_source` is truthy and matches `self.org_integration.integration_id`. Because `AssignmentSource.from_dict` catches errors and returns `None` on invalid input, a malformed `assignment_source_dict` would cause `sync_source` to be `None`, skipping the cycle-prevention check and falling back to config-based syncing. This is an edge-case robustness concern rather than a clearly demonstrated defect in the shown call path (which generally supplies `to_dict()` output).

adjudication_records.issue_text: from_dict only catches ValueError/TypeError; other exceptions propagate into the task

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AssignmentSource.from_dict` only catches `(ValueError, TypeError)`, but the task passes `assignment_source_dict` that is produced by `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, and common malformed inputs (missing/extra keys, non-mapping passed to `**`) would raise `TypeError` which is already caught. The finding asserts that “other exceptions propagate into the task” as a concrete problem, but the diff does not show any realistic path where a different exception would be raised here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cycle guard only covers assignee sync, not status sync — inbound status changes can trigger ping-pong resolve/unresolve loops

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a cycle-prevention check in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` that blocks syncing when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. However, the only call site updated to pass an `AssignmentSource` into `should_sync` is the assignee outbound path (`sync_assignee_outbound` parses `assignment_source_dict` and calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`). For status sync, the diff only updates the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature to accept `assignment_source`, but there’s no shown wiring that passes an `AssignmentSource` into `should_sync` for status attributes or otherwise applies the guard. So the review point that the new cycle guard is currently implemented/used for assignee sync but not demonstrably for status sync is grounded, though the specific claim about actual resolve/unresolve ping-pong loops can’t be verified from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: sync_status_outbound's assignment_source parameter is never passed by any caller, indicating the abstract signature was changed without updating implementations

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` gained an optional `assignment_source` parameter, but it does not show any callers of `sync_status_outbound` at all (only assignee-sync call sites were updated). Therefore the claim that the parameter is “never passed by any caller” is not verifiable from this diff. Also, changing an abstract method’s signature alone does not inherently break implementations unless callers start passing the new kwarg, which is not demonstrated here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Typo in test name test_from_dict_inalid_data
matched_golden_ids: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags a typo in the test name `test_from_dict_inalid_data`, which is exactly the issue described in the golden comment (it should be `test_from_dict_invalid_data`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration can pass even if cycle-protection logic is broken because should_sync returns False before the mock is reached

adjudication.rationale: In the new test, the integration is created with org_integration config including "sync_assignee_outbound": True, and existing tests in the same file already assert that outbound sync occurs for ExampleIntegration, implying `outbound_assignee_key` is set and `org_integration` is present (so `should_sync` does not return False early due to missing key/config). In `sync_assignee_outbound`, the mock is only bypassed if `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` returns False; with config enabled, the only new reason it returns False is the cycle-protection check comparing `sync_source.integration_id` to `self.org_integration.integration_id`. If that cycle-protection logic were broken, `should_sync` would return True and `sync_assignee_outbound` would be called, causing `assert_not_called()` to fail. So the test would not pass if cycle-protection were broken for the same integration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing negative test verifying a non-matching integration still syncs outward

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new conditional logic in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` to skip outbound sync only when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` (to prevent cycles), with an explicit comment that other integrations should still propagate changes outward. Tests were added for the matching-source case (`assert_not_called`) and the default `assignment_source=None` case, but there is no test covering the new branch where a *non-matching* `AssignmentSource` is provided and outbound sync should still occur. That’s a specific missing test for newly added nontrivial behavior.
